title: The Trinity of Markovian Quantum Thermodynamics: Unifying the Axiomatic, Microscopic, and Operational Paradigms
authors: Yutong Luo, Jakub Czartowski, Felix Hubmann, Simon Milz, Felix C. Binder
abstract: Thermodynamics imposes fundamental constraints on the evolution of quantum systems. These constraints and their dynamical consequences have been formulated within distinct paradigms, including axiomatic approaches based on quantum master equations, microscopic descriptions of open-system dynamics, and operational formulations rooted in resource theories. While each perspective has yielded important insights into thermodynamically consistent quantum dynamics, their precise relationship has remained unresolved. Here we establish the exact equivalence of these three paradigms in the Markovian regime. We prove that thermal Lindbladians satisfying Markovianity, time-translation symmetry, and quantum detailed balance are precisely those admitting a microscopic realisation as an energy-conserving thermal collision model and, equivalently, those generating Markovian thermal operations. This unifies the existing approaches to Markovian quantum thermodynamics and identifies its dynamical underpinnings. We further provide an explicit microscopic protocol for simulating thermal Markovian processes with controlled finite-time simulation errors. We illustrate its applicability by providing faithful thermal collision-model implementations of a qubit thermalising in a bosonic environment and of a three-level autonomous thermal machine. In the latter case, the protocol gives rise to a finite-stroke thermal engine that not only reproduces the continuous-time dynamics but also its steady-state thermodynamic performance. As a whole, these results establish a unified foundation for Markovian quantum thermodynamics, showing that its axiomatic, microscopic, and operational formulations are exactly equivalent and providing a universal protocol for implementing thermal processes and machines.
summary: This paper unifies the theory of Markovian quantum thermodynamics by proving the exact equivalence between axiomatic constraints, underlying microscopic collision models, and operational resource theories. It establishes a universal framework for understanding how quantum systems thermalize while providing concrete simulation protocols for implementing these processes. This unification is vital for developing consistent theoretical tools in non-equilibrium quantum physics.
main_problem: The core problem is establishing a rigorous, unified understanding of Markovian quantum thermodynamics by reconciling three distinct theoretical frameworks: axiomatic constraints, microscopic collision models, and operational resource theories.
main_result: The authors prove the exact equivalence between these three paradigms in the Markovian regime, providing a universal foundation for describing thermal processes.
method: The work uses mathematical proofs to establish pairwise equivalences between the generators derived from the axiomatic constraints (e.g., detailed balance), microscopic collision models (ECTCMs), and operational restrictions (MTOs).
model_or_system: The analysis concerns general quantum systems undergoing thermalization via interaction with a bosonic environment, described mathematically by the Lindblad master equation in the Markovian limit.
key_observables: Free energy monotonicity ($F \downarrow$), energy conservation, and the structure of the time-dependent generator $L_t$.
important_parameters: The analysis is restricted to the Markovian regime; finite-time simulation errors are controlled by a specific scaling law.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the system dynamics can be accurately modeled within the memoryless, Markovian approximation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the central theme: the equivalence mapping between the Axiomatic description, the Microscopic (ECTCMs), and the Operational (MTOs) formulations of quantum thermodynamics.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first defining the three paradigms separately, then proving their mutual consistency via mathematical theorems, and finally demonstrating this universality through explicit simulation protocols applied to physical examples like qubit thermalization and autonomous machines.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial theoretical bridge for researchers working on open quantum systems, showing that different seemingly disparate approaches (axiomatic vs. microscopic) converge under specific thermodynamic conditions.
